chapters.title: Mutable default arguments
chapters.subtitle: Python makes a default list when it defines the function.
chapters.body:
## One default object
Python evaluates a default argument when the def statement runs. The function keeps the resulting object.

For `def collect(value, items=[])`, that object is one list. Each call without an items argument uses the same list. The append method changes that list. Thus, a later call sees the values from earlier calls.

Each call has a separate local parameter. Separate parameters can refer to the same object. Assignment does not copy the object.

## A new list for each call
With `items=None`, the function can make a list in each call. The condition `items is None` identifies this case.

If the caller supplies a list, the function uses that list. Changes to this list are visible to the caller.

The expression `items or []` also replaces an empty list from the caller. An empty list is false in a Boolean test. The None condition does not replace it.

## A separate marker
The function can also accept None as input data. In that case, a unique object such as `_MISSING = object()` can identify an absent argument. The identity test `items is _MISSING` does not call custom equality code.

The `function.__defaults__` attribute contains positional defaults. A new function definition makes new default objects.

examples.title: Observe the shared default
examples.code:
def collect(value, items=[]):
    items.append(value)
    return items

first = collect(1)
second = collect(2)
print(first)
print(second)
print(first is second)
print(collect.__defaults__)
examples.explanation: The two results refer to one default list. The second call changes the list that the first result also refers to.

quiz.prompt: When does Python evaluate [] in def f(items=[])?
quiz.explanation: Python evaluates the defaults when the def statement runs.

quiz.prompt: Why can items = items or [] replace caller data?
options: It replaces a valid empty list from the caller
quiz.explanation: An empty list is false in a Boolean test. The caller can supply that list intentionally.

quiz.prompt: Which default can distinguish an absent argument when the function also accepts None?
options: A private object() sentinel checked with is
quiz.explanation: A unique object distinguishes an absent argument from each accepted value.

chapters.title: Equality versus identity
chapters.subtitle: The == operator compares values. The is operator compares object identity.
chapters.body:
## Value and identity
The expression `a == b` tests equality. The expression `a is b` tests whether the two references refer to one object.

Two separate lists can contain equal values. Their equality test gives True, but their identity test gives False.

After `b = a`, the two names refer to the same list. Assignment adds a reference. It does not copy the list.

## A change to an object or a name
The call `a.append(3)` changes the existing list. The two names then show the changed contents.

The assignment `a = [4, 5]` changes which list the name a refers to. The name b refers to the initial list.

For lists, `a += [3]` changes the existing list. The expression `a = a + [3]` makes a different list. Other types can have different rules.

## Special comparisons
The identity test `value is None` identifies the None singleton. A singleton has one object instance.

A class can define value equality through `__eq__`. It cannot change the is operator. NotImplemented tells Python that `__eq__` does not support the other type.

Python can use one integer or string object for multiple references. An identity test does not always give the same result as a value comparison.

A NaN value compares unequal to itself. Its reference is identical to itself.

examples.title: Equal lists and shared references
examples.code:
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = [1, 2, 3]
c = a
print(a == b, a is b)
print(a == c, a is c)
a.append(4)
print(b)
print(c)
examples.explanation: The name b refers to a separate list. The name c refers to the same list as a.

quiz.prompt: Two different lists contain [1, 2]. What is true?
quiz.explanation: The lists have equal contents but different object identities.

quiz.prompt: Why use value is None?
options: It checks the singleton without custom equality
quiz.explanation: The identity test does not call a custom __eq__ method.

quiz.prompt: Does x is y always imply x == y?
options: No. NaN or custom equality can break that implication
quiz.explanation: A NaN reference is identical to itself, but the NaN value compares unequal to itself.

chapters.title: Python slicing
chapters.subtitle: A slice selects sequence positions with start, stop, and step values.
chapters.body:
## Slice positions
The expression `items[start:stop:step]` starts at start. It stops before stop. A positive step moves right. A negative step moves left.

For six items, `[1:5:2]` selects indices 1 and 3. Python limits slice bounds to the available positions. A one index outside the sequence raises IndexError. A slice step of zero raises ValueError.

## Negative steps
The slice `items[::-1]` reverses the sequence. With a negative step, an absent start selects the last item. An absent stop lets the slice include index zero.

An explicit -1 refers to the last item. It differs from an absent stop. Thus, `items[3:-1:-1]` can be empty, while `items[3::-1]` includes the first item.

The method `slice(start, stop, step).indices(len(items))` shows normalized bounds. Those bounds can describe the selected positions with range.

## Copies and changes
A list slice makes a shallow copy. The outer list is new. Nested objects stay shared.

An assignment to a slice changes the existing list. The assignment `items[1:3] = [9]` can change its length.

An extended slice assignment must supply one replacement for each selected position. The reversed function instead gives reverse iteration without a different list.

examples.title: Exclusive stops and reverse defaults
examples.code:
items = list("abcdef")
print(items[1:5:2])
print(items[::-1])
print(items[3::-1])
print(items[3:-1:-1])
print(slice(None, None, -1).indices(len(items)))
examples.explanation: The normalized stop value -1 is a range boundary. It differs from an explicit -1 in the initial slice.

quiz.prompt: Which indices does range(6)[1:5:2] select?
quiz.explanation: The slice excludes its stop at index 5.

quiz.prompt: What does list slicing copy?
options: The outer list and all nested objects
Only the outer list, preserving element references
quiz.explanation: The new outer list keeps references to the existing elements.

quiz.prompt: What happens with a step of zero?
quiz.explanation: A zero step cannot advance through the sequence. Python raises ValueError.

chapters.title: Integer division
chapters.subtitle: The // operator rounds the quotient toward negative infinity.
chapters.body:
## Floor division
In Python 3, `7 / 2` gives the float 3.5. The expression `7 // 2` gives the integer 3.

Floor division rounds toward negative infinity. Thus, `-7 // 2` gives -4. The int conversion instead removes the fractional part toward zero. It gives -3 for -3.5.

If either floor-division operand is a float, the result is usually a float, such as 3.0.

## Quotient and remainder
For integer operands and a nonzero divisor, `a == (a // b) * b + (a % b)`.

For example, `-9 // 2` gives -5. The remainder `-9 % 2` is 1. The calculation `-5 * 2 + 1` gives -9.

A nonzero remainder has the same sign as the divisor. The divmod function gives the quotient and remainder together. Other languages can use different integer-division rules.

## Exact counts
For a nonnegative count n and positive page size, `(n + size - 1) // size` gives the page count. Twenty-one items occupy three pages at ten items per page.

The calculation `int(a / b)` first uses a float. Large integers can lose precision during that calculation. Its treatment of negative results also differs from floor division. A zero divisor raises ZeroDivisionError.

examples.title: Floor is not truncation
examples.code:
print(7 / 2)
print(7 // 2)
print(-7 // 2)
print(int(-7 / 2))
print(7 // -2)
print(7.0 // 2)
examples.explanation: A negative quotient moves toward negative infinity under floor division. Integer conversion moves toward zero.

quiz.prompt: What is -9 // 2?
quiz.explanation: The exact quotient is -4.5. Its floor is -5.

quiz.prompt: What is -9 % 2?
quiz.explanation: The calculation -5 times 2 plus 1 gives -9.

quiz.prompt: Why avoid int(a / b) for exact large-integer division?
options: It uses an inexact float and truncates toward zero
quiz.explanation: The intermediate float can lose precision. Integer conversion also truncates toward zero.

chapters.title: Shallow and deep copying
chapters.subtitle: A shallow copy makes a new outer container. A deep copy also copies nested mutable data.
chapters.body:
## Assignment and shallow copies
The assignment `other = original` gives one object a different name. The two names refer to the same object.

The call original.copy() makes a different outer list. Its elements refer to the initial child objects. This is a shallow copy.

An append to the outer copy does not change the initial outer list. A change to a shared child list is visible through the two containers.

## Deep copies
The copy.deepcopy function copies many nested mutable objects. It keeps a memo of objects that it already copied. This memo supports cycles and keeps repeated references.

If two source positions refer to one child, the copied positions usually refer to one new child. The copied positions can refer to one copied child.

Immutable values can stay shared. Functions and classes do not become separate copies of their definitions. Files and sockets usually have no useful automatic deep copy.

## Repeated rows
The expression `[[0] * 3] * 2` repeats references to one row. A change to one apparent row changes both.

The expression `[[0] * 3 for _ in range(2)]` makes separate rows.

A suitable copy separates the data that must change independently. A change to nested data in the copy can show whether the initial stays unchanged.

examples.title: Three different relationships
examples.code:
from copy import deepcopy
original = [[1, 2]]
alias = original
shallow = original.copy()
deep = deepcopy(original)
shallow[0].append(3)
print(original)
print(deep)
print(alias is original, shallow is original)
print(shallow[0] is original[0])
examples.explanation: The shallow copy has a new outer list. Its child list stays shared with the original.

quiz.prompt: What does list.copy() duplicate?
quiz.explanation: A shallow copy makes a new outer list. It does not copy each child object.

quiz.prompt: Why can [[0]] * 3 surprise you?
options: It makes one shared inner list
quiz.explanation: Sequence multiplication repeats references to one child list.

quiz.prompt: Can deepcopy always make an independent copy of a socket?
options: No. external resources need an explicit policy
quiz.explanation: A file or socket generally has no meaningful automatic deep copy.

chapters.title: Hashability
chapters.subtitle: Hashable objects have stable hashes that agree with equality.
chapters.body:
## Hashable keys
Dictionary keys and set members must be hashable. A hashable object has a stable hash. Equal hashable objects must have equal hashes.

Unequal objects can have the same hash. The container uses equality to distinguish those objects during a lookup.

Lists, dictionaries, and sets are unhashable. A tuple is hashable only when each element is hashable. A tuple that contains an empty list is unhashable.

## Key structure
A tuple can describe an ordered combination, such as country and postcode. A frozenset can describe a collection where order and repeated values do not matter.

A conversion from a list to a tuple changes only the outer sequence. Nested lists stay unhashable. The key uses one consistent rule for case and whitespace when these differences do not identify different records.

## Custom objects
An ordinary class can inherit equality and hashing based on identity. Its attributes can change without a change to identity.

A class with value equality must have a compatible `__hash__` method before its instances can be keys. A change to hash fields after insertion can cause a failed lookup.

Built-in hashes are not unique permanent record identifiers. String hashes can differ between processes. Exact comparisons use full values. A specified deterministic digest gives reproducible disk routing.

examples.title: Ask Python which compound keys are valid
examples.output:
tuple hashable
tuple unhashable
frozenset hashable
list unhashable
examples.explanation: The tuple can have a hash only if each element can have a hash. A list element prevents this.

quiz.prompt: Is a tuple containing a list hashable?
options: No, its list element is unhashable
Only if the list is empty
quiz.explanation: Each tuple element must support a hash. A list does not.

quiz.prompt: Must unequal objects have different hashes?
quiz.explanation: Different keys can have the same hash. Equality distinguishes those keys.

quiz.prompt: Does hash(text) give a permanent identifier across processes?
options: No, it can vary across processes
quiz.explanation: Python can use different string hashes in different processes.

chapters.title: Positional and keyword arguments
chapters.subtitle: The function signature controls how Python assigns arguments to parameters.
chapters.body:
## Parameter rules
Python assigns arguments to parameters before it starts the function body. The caller must supply a value for each required parameter. One parameter cannot receive two values.

Parameters before / are positional-only. Parameters after * or `*args` are keyword-only. A default makes a parameter optional. It does not make the parameter keyword-only.

An option such as overwrite=False states its purpose more clearly than an unexplained positional Boolean.

## Argument collection and expansion
In a definition, `*args` collects extra positional arguments into a tuple. The `**kwargs` parameter collects extra keyword arguments into a dictionary.

At a call, `*values` expands an iterable into positional arguments. The `**options` form expands a mapping with string keys into keyword arguments.

A repeated keyword causes TypeError. A function that passes unknown keywords through many calls can cause an input error far from its source.

## Shared objects
A parameter refers to the supplied object. An append to a list parameter changes the caller's list. A reassignment of the local parameter does not change the caller's variable.

An absent argument can have a different meaning from None or an empty collection. The lifetime rules in Chapter 1 also apply to mutable defaults.

Type annotations describe expected types. They do not enforce runtime types without other validation code.

examples.title: A signature with explicit boundaries
examples.output:
Hello, Ada!
Welcome, Ada.
name must be positional
examples.explanation: The call expands the list and mapping. The function collects the positional values in a tuple.

quiz.prompt: What does *args receive in a definition?
options: A tuple of extra positional arguments
quiz.explanation: The *args parameter collects extra positional arguments in a tuple.

quiz.prompt: What makes an argument keyword-only?
options: It follows * or *args in the signature
quiz.explanation: The signature places keyword-only parameters after * or *args.

quiz.prompt: Do annotations enforce runtime types by themselves?
quiz.explanation: Annotations describe types. Other code must validate runtime values when necessary.

chapters.title: Generators and lazy evaluation
chapters.subtitle: A generator supplies values when the caller requests them.
chapters.body:
## A function that can pause
A call to a function that contains yield makes a generator object. The body starts when iteration first requests a value.

At yield, the function supplies one value and pauses. It keeps its local state. The next request continues after yield. A return or the end of the body finishes iteration.

The caller controls this sequence. The generator does not do parallel work.

## Lazy evaluation
A generator can avoid work on unused input. A request for four results can leave other source values unused.

The list and sorted functions collect their inputs. Thus, sorted(generator) collects the complete input. Caches and readers that fall behind under itertools.tee can also keep values in memory.

A generator is a one-pass iterator. After exhaustion, a different loop receives no values. A new generator or a saved collection permits a different pass.

## Completion and resources
The return statement ends a generator. An explicit StopIteration in its body usually becomes RuntimeError.

The yield from statement delegates iteration and other generator operations to a different generator. That generator's return value is not a different yielded element.

A paused generator can keep a file open. The resource must stay available until consumption finishes. If consumption stops before the end, an explicit close operation can be necessary. Tests with partial consumption can find cleanup failures that a complete list conversion does not show.

examples.title: Observe when the body runs
examples.code:
def numbers():
    print("starting")
    yield 1
    print("resuming")
    yield 2

g = numbers()
print("created")
print(next(g))
print(next(g))
print(list(g))
examples.explanation: The function call makes the generator. The first next call starts its body. The second next call continues after yield.

quiz.prompt: When does a generator function's body start?
quiz.explanation: The first iteration request starts the generator body.

quiz.prompt: Does sorted(generator) stay streaming?
options: Only if the generator uses yield from
quiz.explanation: The sorted function collects the input before it supplies the sorted list.

quiz.prompt: How should a generator end usually?
quiz.explanation: A return or the end of the generator body causes usual exhaustion.

chapters.title: Closures and late binding
chapters.subtitle: A closure keeps access to an enclosing variable and reads its current value.
chapters.body:
## Enclosing variables
A nested function can use a variable from its enclosing function after the outer call finishes. The function and its environment form a closure.

The closure usually reads the current value of the variable when the closure runs. It does not automatically keep a fixed value from its definition.

## Callbacks in a loop
A loop changes one variable i. Each iteration does not make a new function scope. Thus, callbacks that read i after the loop see its final value.

This behavior applies to def and lambda functions. A module variable can cause the same delayed-lookup error outside a closure.

## Separate captured values
The expression `lambda i=i: i` keeps the current object as a default argument. A separate factory call for each callback makes a separate enclosing variable.

The functools.partial function can also assign arguments in advance. These methods keep object references. They do not make mutable data immutable.

A change to a captured list stays visible to the callback. An applicable copy can give a snapshot with no shared mutable data.

## Name lookup
The nonlocal statement permits reassignment of an existing enclosing variable. This declaration is not necessary for a read or a change to a referenced list.

Ordinary name lookup searches local, enclosing, module-global, and built-in scopes. Assignment usually makes a name local throughout a function. A read before that local assignment raises UnboundLocalError.

examples.title: The loop captures one changing binding
examples.code:
def build():
    callbacks = []
    for i in range(3):
        callbacks.append(lambda: i)
    return callbacks

print([f() for f in build()])
fixed = [lambda i=i: i for i in range(3)]
print([f() for f in fixed])
examples.explanation: The first callbacks share one variable i. Each corrected callback has its own default value.

quiz.prompt: Is late binding specific to lambdas?
options: No, nested def functions can show it too
quiz.explanation: The two lambda and def functions can read the same changing variable.

quiz.prompt: What does lambda i=i: i capture?
options: The current object as a default value
quiz.explanation: The default keeps the current object reference. It does not copy the object graph.

quiz.prompt: What gives each callback its own enclosing binding?
options: Calling a factory once per callback
quiz.explanation: Each factory call makes a different enclosing environment.

chapters.title: Decorators and functools.wraps
chapters.subtitle: A decorator replaces a function with a different callable object.
chapters.body:
## Definition and call time
The decorator syntax @decorate is approximately equivalent to function = decorate(function).

Python first makes the initial function. It passes that function to the decorator. The name then refers to the object that the decorator returns.

Decoration occurs when the definition runs. A returned wrapper runs later, when a caller calls the decorated function.

## Results and metadata
A wrapper commonly accepts `*args` and `**kwargs`. It calls the initial function and returns the result. Without a return statement, the caller receives None.

The functools.wraps decorator keeps useful metadata and supplies `__wrapped__` for inspection. It does not enforce types or add thread safety.

An async wrapper usually awaits its initial async function. A generator wrapper must keep lazy behavior if callers use it. A try/finally statement contains necessary cleanup.

## Decorator order
With @outer above @inner, Python makes outer(inner(function)). At call time, the outer wrapper starts first.

A cache outside an authorization check can prevent that check on a cache hit. The order must agree with the operations that must occur on each call.

A configured decorator such as repeat(3) adds a factory call. The factory receives configuration and returns a decorator. That decorator receives the function and returns the wrapper.

examples.title: Wrap without losing the result or name
examples.explanation: The wrapper returns the initial result. The wraps decorator keeps the initial function name.

quiz.prompt: What does Python build with @a above @b?
options: a and b run in parallel
quiz.explanation: The nearest decorator receives the initial function first. The result then passes to the outer decorator.

quiz.prompt: What does wraps mainly keep?
quiz.explanation: The wraps decorator copies useful metadata and supplies __wrapped__.

quiz.prompt: What happens if a wrapper omits return?
options: The initial result is returned automatically
quiz.explanation: Without an explicit return, a function returns None.

chapters.title: Class versus instance attributes
chapters.subtitle: A class attribute can be shared. An instance attribute belongs to one instance.
chapters.body:
## Attribute lookup
For a plain attribute, an instance searches its own attributes and then its class hierarchy. Multiple instances can refer to one class attribute without copies.

Descriptors, such as properties, add other lookup rules. The simple rule here applies to plain attributes.

## One shared list
The definition `class Team: members = []` makes one class list. An instance without its own members attribute finds that shared list.

The append method changes the list. It does not make an attribute in the instance dictionary. Thus, a different instance can see the new element.

An assignment `self.members = []` in `__init__` makes a separate list for each instance. A shared registry or immutable configuration value can instead belong to the class.

## Assignment and change
For a plain attribute, `team.kind = "research"` makes an instance attribute. This attribute takes priority over the class value for that instance.

Other instances find the class value. Deletion of the instance attribute makes the class value visible again.

The += operation on an inherited list can change the shared object before assignment to the instance. Subclasses can also share inherited mutable class data.

A constructor that receives a list must have a clear copy policy. It can keep the caller's list or make an applicable copy.

examples.title: A class list is shared
examples.code:
class Team:
    members = []

a = Team()
b = Team()
a.members.append("Ada")
print(b.members)
print(a.members is b.members)
print("members" in a.__dict__)
examples.explanation: The lookup finds the class list. The append method changes that list without an assignment to the instance.

quiz.prompt: Where should an independent mutable list usually be made?
quiz.explanation: The initializer can make a different list for each instance.

quiz.prompt: Does a.items.append(x) make a.items in a.__dict__?
options: No, it can mutate an inherited list
quiz.explanation: The method changes the object that lookup finds. It does not assign an instance attribute.

quiz.prompt: What does a.kind = "x" usually do for a plain class attribute?
quiz.explanation: For a plain attribute, the new instance value takes priority over the class value.

chapters.title: Equality and hashing contracts
chapters.subtitle: Equal hashable objects must have equal hashes.
chapters.body:
## Value equality
The class definition must state which fields determine equality. A coordinate can compare x and y. A database entity can compare a stable identifier.

The `__eq__` method returns NotImplemented when it does not support the other type. Python can then try the other operand. NotImplementedError does not request this fallback.

## Compatible hashes
For hashable values, if a == b, then hash(a) == hash(b). The reverse condition can be false. Unequal values can have the same hash.

The hash must use the same stable fields as equality. An extra hash field that equality ignores can give equal objects different hashes.

A class that defines `__eq__` without a compatible `__hash__` usually becomes unhashable. This prevents identity hashing from disagreeing with value equality.

## Stable keys
A change to a key's hash after insertion can cause lookup to search a different location. A change to equality fields is also unsafe.

Immutable value objects avoid this failure when their fields are stable. A comparison policy must also state whether subclasses can compare equal to the base type.

Generated dataclass equality compares values only for the same concrete class. A useful test inserts one instance as a dictionary key. A separate equal instance must retrieve the same value. The test does not specify a numeric hash value.

examples.title: An immutable value key
examples.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Point:
    x: int
    y: int

a = Point(2, 3)
b = Point(2, 3)
print(a == b, a is b)
print(hash(a) == hash(b))
print({a: "home"}[b])
examples.explanation: The frozen dataclass generates compatible equality and hashing for these fields. A separate equal instance can retrieve the dictionary value.

quiz.prompt: Which rule must equal hashable objects obey?
options: Equal hashable objects imply equal hashes
quiz.explanation: Equal hashable keys must have equal hashes. Hash collisions stay permitted for unequal keys.

quiz.prompt: What should unsupported __eq__ return?
quiz.explanation: NotImplemented lets Python try a different comparison implementation.

quiz.prompt: What is the usual result of defining __eq__ without __hash__?
quiz.explanation: Python disables the inherited identity hash after a class defines value equality without a compatible hash.

chapters.title: Multiple inheritance and MRO
chapters.subtitle: The method resolution order determines the next method that super calls.
chapters.body:
## One lookup sequence
Python uses C3 linearization for multiple inheritance. The result is the method resolution order, or MRO. `Class.__mro__` and Class.mro() show this sequence.

The MRO keeps local base order and established ancestor order. A shared ancestor occurs once in a diamond. Inconsistent order requirements cause TypeError during class creation.

## The next implementation
In a method, super uses the defining class and the actual instance. It searches after that class in the instance's MRO.

A diamond can have the sequence D, B, C, A, object. On a D instance, a super call in B then continues to C. It does not always select B's directly declared parent.

If each method calls super once, the chain can visit each implementation once. Direct calls to named base methods can skip implementations or repeat a shared ancestor.

## Compatible arguments
A constructor can consume its own keyword arguments. It passes the remaining arguments to super. The final call to `object.__init__` must have no unsupported arguments.

A method without a super call ends the chain. This must agree with the behavior of the other bases.

The MRO is useful evidence for unexpected dispatch. A different base order can change behavior. Separate helper objects can be simpler for independent responsibilities.

examples.title: Trace a diamond cooperatively
examples.explanation: The super call in B continues to C for this D instance. The next super call continues to A.

quiz.prompt: What does super() select in a cooperative method?
options: The next implementation in the instance's MRO
quiz.explanation: The actual instance MRO determines the next method.

quiz.prompt: How often does a shared ancestor appear in the MRO?
quiz.explanation: The linearized order contains each ancestor once.

quiz.prompt: What happens when Python cannot form a consistent MRO?
quiz.explanation: Python rejects class definitions with inconsistent order requirements.

chapters.title: The iteration protocol
chapters.subtitle: A for loop requests values from an iterator until the iterator reports exhaustion.
chapters.body:
## Iterable and iterator
An iterable can supply an iterator. An iterator keeps a current position. The next operation requests a different value. StopIteration reports exhaustion.

A list can supply several independent iterators. For an iterator it, iter(it) gives the same iterator.

A for loop gets an iterator from its source. It requests values until exhaustion. This protocol supports lists, files, generators, and custom sources.

## Consumption
The sum and list functions consume iterator values. Loops and membership tests can also consume values.

After sum(g), list(g) receives only the remaining values. An exhausted generator gives an empty list. A new iterator or an applicable saved collection permits a second pass.

The form next(it, default) supplies a value for exhaustion. Other errors during value production stay failures.

## Custom behavior and tools
An iterator implements `__iter__` with self as the result. Its `__next__` method advances its state. After exhaustion, the iterator must stay exhausted.

A reusable collection instead supplies a new iterator. The zip function stops at the shortest input by default. Its strict=True option checks length agreement.

The tee function supplies multiple readers but keeps a buffer when one reader falls behind. The source must stay available for lazy consumption. A file iterator cannot read data after its file closes.

examples.title: An iterator remembers its position
examples.code:
values = [10, 20, 30]
it = iter(values)
print(next(it))
print(list(it))
print(list(it))
print(list(values))
print(next(it, "finished"))
examples.explanation: The iterator advances through the source list. This does not remove elements from the source list.

quiz.prompt: What does iter(it) return for an iterator it?
quiz.explanation: The iterator __iter__ method returns self.

quiz.prompt: Why can sum(g); list(g) produce an empty list?
quiz.explanation: The sum operation consumes the iterator. No values stay after exhaustion.

quiz.prompt: What does zip stop at by default?
quiz.explanation: The default zip behavior stops when the shortest input finishes.

chapters.title: Subclass registration
chapters.subtitle: The __init_subclass__ hook runs when Python makes a subclass.
chapters.body:
## Class creation
A base class can define `__init_subclass__` to inspect or configure each new subclass. The cls parameter refers to the new subclass.

The hook runs when the class statement makes the subclass. It does not run for each new instance. The hook already has its special class-method behavior without an explicit classmethod decorator.

## A class registry
A subclass definition can supply a keyword such as format_name="json". The hook can check this name and keep the class in a registry.

Later, application code selects the class and makes an instance. The registry must use stable names and state a rule for duplicate names.

A duplicate error prevents import order from silently replacing an implementation. A registry dictionary on the base stays shared unless a different class makes a separate dictionary.

## Cooperation and discovery
The hook consumes the class keywords that it owns. It passes the remaining keywords through super().`__init_subclass__`. Other bases can use these keywords.

Unsupported keywords that reach object cause an error. Registration occurs only after the intended class definitions execute. A registry does not discover modules before import.

Class creation is a suitable time for small checks and registration. Network requests and resource acquisition belong to explicit runtime operations. An ordinary registration function is an alternative when class-creation effects become difficult to follow.

examples.title: Register subclasses by a declared key
examples.explanation: The class definition registers Upper. Application code makes the selected instance in a separate operation.

quiz.prompt: When does __init_subclass__ run?
options: Only when the base is deleted
quiz.explanation: The hook runs during subclass creation, not instance creation.

quiz.prompt: Does a registry automatically discover unimported modules?
quiz.explanation: The implementation modules must execute their class definitions first.

quiz.prompt: Why forward remaining class keywords with super?
options: To participate in other bases' hooks
quiz.explanation: Each base consumes its own options and passes other options to the next hook.

chapters.title: Dataclasses and default factories
chapters.subtitle: A dataclass can make common methods and a separate mutable default for each instance.
chapters.body:
## Generated methods
The dataclass decorator reads annotated fields. It can generate `__init__`, `__repr__`, and `__eq__`. The result stays an ordinary class.

Annotations do not validate runtime types automatically. The generated initializer calls `__post_init__` if that method exists. This method can check relationships between fields.

The initializer does not automatically call an ordinary non-dataclass base initializer.

## Default factories
The declaration field(default_factory=list) makes a separate default list for each instance. The factory must be the callable list, not the result of list().

The initializer calls the factory when the caller does not supply the field. If the caller supplies a list, the instance usually keeps that reference. The factory does not copy explicit arguments.

## Frozen instances
The option frozen=True prevents ordinary field reassignment. It does not make contained objects immutable. A list in a frozen instance can change.

Generated equality compares fields only for the same concrete class. It compares the participating fields. The compare=False option excludes a field.

A mutable dataclass with value equality is usually unhashable. A frozen dataclass can receive a generated hash if its fields support hashes. The unsafe_hash option does not make mutable key data safe.

The dataclasses.replace function makes a different instance. It does not deep-copy unchanged fields. Mutable nested values can stay shared.

examples.title: Each instance gets its own default list
examples.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class Notebook:
    title: str
    pages: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)

a = Notebook("A")
b = Notebook("B")
a.pages.append("objects")
print(a.pages, b.pages)
print(a.pages is b.pages)
examples.explanation: The initializer calls list separately for each absent pages argument. The two instances have different default lists.

quiz.prompt: Which field declaration makes an independent list default?
quiz.explanation: The factory must be a zero-argument callable.

quiz.prompt: Does frozen=True freeze an inner list?
options: Only if the list has strings
quiz.explanation: The field reference cannot change through ordinary assignment. The contained list can change.

quiz.prompt: Do dataclass annotations validate input at runtime?
quiz.explanation: Annotations alone do not validate runtime values.

chapters.title: Caching instance methods
chapters.subtitle: A method cache includes self in its keys and can keep an instance alive.
chapters.body:
## Method cache keys
The lru_cache decorator makes a wrapper on the class. A bound method call supplies self as an argument. Thus, self is part of the cache key and must be hashable.

The wrapper shares one cache capacity across instances. It does not make a private cache for each instance. Different instances usually use different keys unless their equality makes them equivalent.

## Retained references
The cache keeps arguments and results until eviction or a cache-clear operation. A reference to self can keep an instance alive after other references disappear.

The maxsize parameter limits entries, not bytes. One entry can keep a large object graph alive. With maxsize=None, the entry count has no limit.

## Old results
A method can read mutable instance fields. If those fields change but the key stays equal, the cache can return an old result.

Stable inputs, an immutable version value, or explicit invalidation can prevent this error. A changed object hash is not a safe way to force a different calculation.

A cached_property keeps one value on the instance. Deletion of that attribute permits a new calculation. It does not cache parameterized calls.

The lru_cache structure stays coherent across threads. However, concurrent misses can calculate the same result twice. The cache does not guarantee one execution of a side effect.

examples.title: self divides the cache key space
examples.code:
from functools import lru_cache

class Scale:
    def __init__(self, factor):
        self.factor = factor
    @lru_cache(maxsize=4)
    def apply(self, value):
        print("computing")
        return self.factor * value

a, b = Scale(2), Scale(3)
print(a.apply(5))
print(a.apply(5))
print(b.apply(5))
print(Scale.apply.cache_info().hits)
Scale.apply.cache_clear()
examples.explanation: The instances a and b use separate keys. Only the second call on a is a cache hit.

quiz.prompt: Does self participate in an lru_cache method key?
quiz.explanation: A bound method call includes self among the wrapper arguments.

quiz.prompt: Does maxsize limit the number of bytes that a cache keeps?
quiz.explanation: An entry can keep references to a large object graph.

quiz.prompt: Can two threads compute the same missing key?
quiz.explanation: The cache keeps coherent internal state but can repeat a calculation after concurrent misses.

chapters.title: Lists versus sets
chapters.subtitle: A list keeps order and repeated values. A set represents different members.
chapters.body:
## Different data requirements
A list keeps sequence order, repeated values, and indexed positions. A set keeps different hashable members. A conversion to a set can remove information that the application uses.

List membership can compare values one at a time. It can do up to O(n) comparisons.

Set lookup has expected O(1) cost for ordinary well-distributed keys. Severe hash collisions can increase this cost toward O(n). These estimates assume bounded costs for hashes and equality.

## Construction cost
Set construction takes expected O(n) time and uses more memory. A scan of a small list can cost less for one query.

Repeated queries can use one set that the program makes in advance. A new set(values) for each query repeats the construction cost.

Big-O describes growth. It does not give the faster structure for each input size or computer.

## Equality and order
The values 1, True, and 1.0 compare equal and have equal hashes. They occupy one logical set entry. A key that includes type can distinguish them when necessary.

A set does not promise insertion order. A membership set and an output list can keep first-seen order. For hashable values, list(dict.fromkeys(values)) is a different option.

A persistent list and set that represent one collection must have consistent updates. A temporary set from a stable list can avoid this requirement.

examples.title: Order-preserving deduplication
examples.code:
values = ["b", "a", "b", "c", "a"]
unique = list(dict.fromkeys(values))
print(unique)
print("a" in set(values))
print(len({1, True, 1.0}))
examples.explanation: Dictionary keys keep first insertion order. The three numeric forms compare equal, so the set contains one member.

quiz.prompt: Is set membership guaranteed O(1) in each case?
options: No, expected O(1) with possible collision degradation
quiz.explanation: Severe collisions can increase lookup cost. Hash and equality calculations can also be expensive.

quiz.prompt: What can set(values) lose?
quiz.explanation: A set represents different membership. It does not keep sequence order or duplicates.

quiz.prompt: How should repeated lookups use an index?
options: Build the same set for each lookup
Build it once and reuse it
quiz.explanation: One construction lets later queries use the existing membership set.

chapters.title: Insertion complexity
chapters.subtitle: An insertion at the front of a list moves the existing references.
chapters.body:
## Front insertion
A CPython list contains a resizable array of object references. An insertion at position zero moves existing references to make space.

The program does not deep-copy the referenced objects. However, movement of n references takes O(n) work. An insertion in the middle moves the remaining part of the array.

Repeated front insertion for n values moves approximately 0 + 1 + ... + n - 1 references. The total cost is O(n²).

## Append cost
An append usually uses spare capacity. Sometimes the array must grow and move its references. A one append can therefore take O(n) work.

Across a sequence of n appends, total work is O(n). This gives amortized O(1) cost per append. It does not promise equal time for each operation.

## Queues and construction order
The collections.deque type supports efficient additions and removals at the two ends. The append and popleft methods implement first-in, first-out processing.

A deque does not give constant-time access to an arbitrary middle position.

If front insertion only makes a reversed sequence, appends followed by one reverse operation give the same result with linear total work.

The list itself holds references. Its elements can use more memory. A performance comparison must include the actual operations and the same output order.

examples.title: Use a deque for a FIFO queue
examples.code:
from collections import deque
queue = deque(["first", "second"])
queue.append("third")
print(queue.popleft())
print(list(queue))
queue.appendleft("urgent")
print(list(queue))
examples.explanation: The deque processes a first-in, first-out queue. Removal from its left end avoids repeated shifts of list references.

quiz.prompt: What is the usual cost of list.insert(0, x) for length n?
quiz.explanation: The insertion moves the existing references to make space.

quiz.prompt: What does amortized O(1) mean for append?
options: Total work across many appends is linear
quiz.explanation: A sequence of n appends takes linear total work, despite some expensive individual appends.

quiz.prompt: Which structure fits repeated FIFO append/popleft?
quiz.explanation: A deque supports efficient append and popleft operations.

chapters.title: Sorting stability
chapters.subtitle: A stable sort keeps the relative order of records with equal keys.
chapters.body:
## Equal-key records
Python sorted and list.sort are stable. Students with equal grades keep their previous relative order after a sort by grade.

Python uses an adaptive stable implementation commonly called Timsort. It can use existing ordered runs. Its usual worst-case comparison growth is O(n log n). Favorable input can take linear work.

Key construction and comparisons also have costs.

## New list or changed list
The sorted function makes a new list. The list.sort method changes the existing list and returns None. Other references to that list see the new order.

A key function runs once for each item. Its results must permit the specified comparisons. Side effects can make the operation difficult to understand.

## Multiple priorities
A tuple key such as department and score compares the first field first. It compares the next field when the first fields are equal.

Stable passes also support mixed directions. The secondary key comes first. The primary key comes last. The final pass keeps secondary order within each primary group.

The reverse=True option also keeps stability. A reverse operation after an ascending sort can instead reverse tied records.

Stability keeps the input tie order. An more key such as an identifier can give deterministic output from arbitrary input order. A complete sort collects all input from a generator.

examples.title: Stable ties preserve input order
examples.code:
rows = [("Ada", 90), ("Grace", 80), ("Lin", 90)]
ordered = sorted(rows, key=lambda row: row[1])
print(ordered)
print(rows)
examples.explanation: Ada stays before Lin among the equal 90-point records. The sorted function leaves the source list unchanged.

quiz.prompt: What does a stable sort keep?
quiz.explanation: Stability keeps relative order only within equal-key groups.

quiz.prompt: What does list.sort return?
quiz.explanation: The sort method changes its list and returns None.

quiz.prompt: For stable multi-pass sorting, which key is sorted last?
quiz.explanation: The final primary pass keeps the earlier secondary order within each primary group.

chapters.title: The Two Sum algorithm
chapters.subtitle: Two Sum finds two different positions whose values add to a target.
chapters.body:
## Result requirements
The two indices must differ. The two values can be equal. These examples return the first pair found in a left-to-right scan, or None.

A search through each pair takes O(n²) time. A dictionary can avoid repeated searches through earlier values.

## The complement lookup
For a current value x, the partner value is target - x. The dictionary maps earlier values to their indices.

The algorithm looks for the partner before it inserts x. A found index therefore belongs to an earlier position. The current element cannot match itself.

Before each iteration, the dictionary contains only processed positions. This is the loop invariant. It explains why a result uses different positions and why earlier partners stay available.

## Repeated values and cost
For [3, 3] with target 6, the algorithm first keeps the index of the first 3. The second 3 then finds that entry.

Insertion before the lookup could permit a one value to match itself. The setdefault method keeps the earliest stored index. Replacement of an index can change which correct pair the function returns.

With ordinary keys, expected time is O(n) and extra space is O(n). Severe collisions can increase the time. Floating-point approximate sums must use their own defined comparison rule.

examples.title: Find a pair using only earlier values
examples.explanation: The lookup occurs before insertion. An equal earlier value can match, but the current index cannot match itself.

quiz.prompt: Why look up before inserting the current value?
options: To prevent using the same index twice
quiz.explanation: The dictionary must contain only earlier positions at the lookup.

quiz.prompt: Does [3, 3] contain a valid pair for target 6?
quiz.explanation: Different indices can contain equal values.

quiz.prompt: What is the expected time with ordinary dictionary keys?
quiz.explanation: The algorithm does one expected-constant-time lookup and insertion per value.

chapters.title: Heaps and Top-K selection
chapters.subtitle: A heap can select a small result without a complete sort of the input.
chapters.body:
## Heap order
In a min-heap, each parent is no greater than its children. The smallest value is at index zero. The full array is not sorted.

The heapify operation takes O(n) time. A push or pop takes O(log n) time because it repairs one tree path. Binary search does not apply to the heap array.

## A small selection
The heapq.nsmallest function returns the k smallest values in sorted order. For small k relative to n, heap selection commonly takes O(n log k) time and O(k) space.

The helper has special paths. It can use a minimum for one result and a full sort for a large selection. When k approaches n, a full sort can be simpler and faster.

## The largest k values
A min-heap can keep the largest k candidates. After the heap becomes full, its root is the smallest selected value. This is the cutoff.

A new value below the cutoff does not enter the result. A larger value can replace the root through heapreplace. A final sort can arrange the selected output.

Record selection can use a key function. A priority queue can use a counter to resolve equal priorities without payload comparisons. The result requirements must specify whether ties can increase the result beyond k items.

examples.title: Select without fully ordering each input
examples.code:
import heapq
values = [9, 1, 8, 2, 7, 3, 6]
print(heapq.nsmallest(3, values))
print(heapq.nlargest(2, values))
heapq.heapify(values)
print(values[0])
print(heapq.heappop(values))
examples.explanation: The heap root is the smallest value. Other heap positions do not have a complete sorted order.

quiz.prompt: Is a heap array fully sorted?
options: No, it satisfies a parent/child invariant
quiz.explanation: The parent-child rule does not fully order all array positions.

quiz.prompt: Which structure keeps the largest k using a cutoff at its root?
options: An unsorted tuple of all values
quiz.explanation: The smallest retained value is the cutoff for a larger new candidate.

quiz.prompt: When is a full sort often preferable?
options: When k is close to n
quiz.explanation: The selection benefit becomes smaller when the requested output approaches the whole input.

chapters.title: Hash invariants and collisions
chapters.subtitle: A hash finds possible keys. Equality identifies the correct key.
chapters.body:
## Hash collisions
A dictionary uses a hash to find candidate keys. Equality distinguishes the candidates.

Different values can have the same hash. They can stay separate dictionary entries. Equal hashable values, however, must have equal hashes.

If equal keys have different hashes, lookup can search the wrong location.

## Stable key data
Hash fields and equality fields must stay stable while a key is in the dictionary. A change after insertion can cause lookup failures.

A constant-hash class can stay correct if its equality is correct. It can be slow because lookup compares many candidates.

Ordinary well-distributed keys give expected O(1) lookup. Severe collisions can increase this cost toward O(n).

## Equality controls different entries
The values 1 and True compare equal and have equal hashes. An assignment with either value updates one logical entry. A compound key can include type when the application must keep different entries.

Containers can recognize an identical key without ordinary value comparison. This matters for special values such as NaN.

## Exact identification
Built-in hashes are not unique permanent identifiers. Some hashes also differ between processes.

Exact deduplication must compare full normalized values. A deterministic digest can route records to disk partitions. A digest collision must not cause unequal initial records to become one record.

examples.title: Colliding keys stay different
examples.explanation: All keys have the same hash in this example. Equality distinguishes the values a and b.

quiz.prompt: Do equal hashes prove equal values?
quiz.explanation: Hash collisions do not prove equality.

quiz.prompt: What does a constant __hash__ primarily harm if equality is correct?
quiz.explanation: Equal-key lookup stays correct, but many candidates can make it slow.

quiz.prompt: What is required for exact disk deduplication?
options: Compare full canonical values after routing
quiz.explanation: A routing hash must not replace the initial value in an exact comparison.

chapters.title: External-memory algorithms
chapters.subtitle: Disk partitions permit exact deduplication when the full working set exceeds RAM.
chapters.body:
## Separate disk partitions
Strings, references, and hash-table capacity can make an ID set larger than the raw input file. A full in-memory set can exceed RAM.

Hash partitioning separates the input into disk shards. Each shard must fit the available memory for its deduplication step.

The program first normalizes each ID under one consistent rule. A deterministic function then sends equal normalized IDs to the same shard.

Different IDs can enter one shard. This is safe because the deduplication step compares their full values.

## The largest shard
The program reads one fitting shard, removes duplicate full IDs, and writes the different results. The memory estimate must include object overhead and the number of different IDs.

An uneven distribution can make one shard too large. More digest bits can repartition that shard. External sorting is a different option. The same routing rule alone does not guarantee smaller partitions.

Built-in string hashes can differ between processes. A specified digest such as BLAKE2 gives reproducible routing. A Bloom filter alone cannot guarantee exact results because false positives can discard new values.

## Output and recovery
Combined shard output does not keep first-seen order. Earliest positions and a different ordering step can keep that order.

The process must limit open files and batch writes. It must have temporary disk space and a record of completed stages.

examples.title: Route deterministically, compare full IDs
examples.code:
from hashlib import blake2b

def shard_for(value, count):
    digest = blake2b(value.encode("utf-8"), digest_size=8).digest()
    return int.from_bytes(digest, "big") % count

ids = ["a", "b", "a", "c", "b"]
shards = [[] for _ in range(4)]
for value in ids:
    shards[shard_for(value, len(shards))].append(value)
unique = set()
for shard in shards:
    unique.update(set(shard))
print(sorted(unique))
print(shard_for("a", 4) == shard_for("a", 4))
examples.explanation: This small in-memory example shows deterministic routing. A large implementation writes and reads the shards on disk.

quiz.prompt: Why does shard-by-shard deduplication work?
options: Equal canonical IDs route to the same shard
Each shard has the same size
quiz.explanation: All occurrences of an equal normalized ID reach one shard.

quiz.prompt: What should happen to an oversized shard?
options: Repartition with more distinguishing bits or externally sort it
quiz.explanation: The largest shard must fit the available memory. More partitioning or external sorting can reduce the working set.

quiz.prompt: Does shard concatenation keep first-seen order?
options: No, that needs more sequence metadata and ordering
quiz.explanation: Shard order differs from input order. Earliest-position data and a different ordering step can keep first-seen order.

chapters.title: Extract Function refactoring
chapters.subtitle: Extract Function moves one complete operation into a named function.
chapters.body:
## One implementation of a rule
Repeated validation can change differently in separate locations. A shared function gives that rule one implementation.

The function name states the operation that the caller uses. Two business rules can use similar syntax but have different meanings.

## Behavior must stay the same
A structural refactor keeps return values, errors, data changes, and relevant operation order. If two checks fail, their order determines the first reported error.

A changed validation policy is a separate behavior change. A combined change makes failure causes more difficult to identify.

The extracted function must have clear inputs and results. Explicit arguments avoid new dependencies on hidden global state.

## Related actions
Validation examines data. Normalization changes its form. If a function does the two, its name must describe the two actions.

Many Boolean switches can indicate unrelated policies in one helper. A registration name and a display label can have different rules, even if the two currently contain strings.

A safe change sequence starts with one caller and a behavior check. Other callers then use the new function. The old duplicate implementations no longer remain.

Tests through the public callers show whether correct inputs, incorrect inputs, and empty inputs keep their previous behavior. The result is one rule that is easier to find without a change to its meaning.

examples.title: One owner for a shared validation rule
examples.explanation: The two callers use the same function. That function removes outer whitespace and rejects an empty name.

quiz.prompt: Which observations must stay the same after a behavior-preserving extraction?
options: Outputs, errors, mutation, and relevant ordering
quiz.explanation: Callers can observe errors, data changes, and operation order as well as return values.

quiz.prompt: What can many Boolean switches in the helper indicate?
quiz.explanation: Similar syntax can hide different business rules.

quiz.prompt: What does a useful extracted function name describe?
options: A name describing the complete operation
The first variable in the old block
quiz.explanation: A complete operation name states why the caller uses the helper.

chapters.title: Polymorphism and conditional replacement
chapters.subtitle: Polymorphism lets different objects give the same operation.
chapters.body:
## Repeated type decisions
Several consumers can contain the same type tests before a render operation. A new document type then causes changes in each consumer.

An alternative gives each implementation a render method. Consumers call that method directly. This is polymorphism.

Python supports polymorphism through inheritance, Protocols, or compatible objects without a shared base class.

## A common operation
Each old branch moves into its related implementation. Its results and errors stay the same. Consumers then use the common operation instead of repeated type tests.

A one setup location can choose the implementation. Polymorphism can keep some conditionals.

Small stateless transformations can use a dictionary of functions instead of several classes.

## Compatible behavior
A shared method name does not prove compatibility. A renderer that returns text differs from one that writes a file and returns None.

Implementations must use the same input meanings and output requirements. Their errors and effects on caller data must also agree.

Concrete-type tests in consumers can indicate exceptions to these rules. The common operation must then have a clearer definition.

A one conditional over a small fixed choice can stay simpler. Tests must examine each implementation's behavior and the setup decision independently. A correct implementation cannot help if setup selects the wrong one.

examples.title: Call behavior without checking types
examples.explanation: The publish function calls render. It does not test the renderer type.

quiz.prompt: Does polymorphism require a common base class in Python?
options: No, compatible behavior can be structural
quiz.explanation: Compatible behavior can support structural polymorphism without inheritance.

quiz.prompt: Must each conditional disappear?
options: No, selection can stay at a boundary
Only if there are three classes
quiz.explanation: One setup decision can stay while consumers stop repeating type checks.

quiz.prompt: When might a function table be better?
options: When each case has unrelated outputs
quiz.explanation: Functions can represent small stateless alternatives without more classes.

chapters.title: SOLID: Open/Closed and Liskov Substitution
chapters.subtitle: Extensions must keep the behavior that existing callers use.
chapters.body:
## Open/Closed
A pricing function can accept a discount policy. A new policy can work without a different branch in the pricing function. Application setup selects the policy.

The Open/Closed Principle supports an extension point for a real variation. It does not prohibit all changes to existing files.

## Liskov Substitution
A replacement must accept the promised inputs and supply the promised results. A matching method name or signature is not sufficient.

A subtype must not strengthen preconditions. If a reader accepts all nonnegative counts, a subtype cannot reject counts greater than ten without violating that requirement.

A subtype must not weaken successful guarantees. A writer that promises data retention cannot silently discard writes. Errors and side effects also form part of the specified behavior.

## Behavior before categories
A mutable rectangle can permit independent width and height assignments. A square that changes the two dimensions on either assignment violates that interface.

The mathematical relationship does not prove software substitutability. A smaller immutable shape interface that supplies area can support the two types.

Protocols and type checkers examine structural compatibility. They do not prove all behavior. Data retention and changes to caller data must have their own evidence.

A small interface with clear requirements is easier for each implementation to support. Separate interfaces can help when implementations cannot support the same usual operations.

examples.title: Extend a consumer through a policy
examples.explanation: The invoice function accepts a supplied policy. Each policy supplies the amount calculation.

quiz.prompt: Does Open/Closed mean existing code may never be edited?
options: No, it guides a chosen extension boundary
quiz.explanation: The principle supports a chosen extension point. It does not prohibit maintenance.

quiz.prompt: Can a subtype reject inputs the base contract accepts?
options: That strengthens preconditions and can break substitution
Only if it has more methods
quiz.explanation: A valid caller must stay valid with the replacement implementation.

quiz.prompt: Does matching a Protocol prove semantic substitutability?
options: No, behavioral obligations need reasoning and tests
quiz.explanation: A matching structure does not prove that an implementation keeps its behavioral promises.

chapters.title: The Strategy pattern
chapters.subtitle: A strategy is a supplied algorithm that a consumer can replace.
chapters.body:
## Separate the algorithm
A checkout can use a standard shipping calculation or an express shipping calculation. The checkout adds the result. The supplied strategy determines the formula.

Setup can select the strategy, or the caller can supply it per call. The strategy can stay the same throughout execution.

## Functions and callable objects
A small stateless strategy can be a function. A callable object can keep configuration or state with the algorithm. A strategy can work without a common base class.

The consumer calls the shared operation. Concrete-type tests in the consumer would repeat the initial selection problem.

## Required behavior
Strategies must have compatible input meanings, result types, errors, and data-change rules. An unexpected change to caller input can break compatibility despite equal signatures.

A price strategy must also specify units and a rounding rule. Integer minor units distinguish pounds from pence but do not determine each fraction rule.

A clear setup or call location selects the implementation. A test can supply a deterministic strategy and examine the consumer result. Separate tests can examine independent algorithm rules.

Strategy usually uses composition. Template Method uses inherited steps in a fixed sequence. The variation determines which design is suitable. A callback can work without a class hierarchy.

examples.title: Functions as shipping strategies
examples.explanation: The checkout adds the subtotal and shipping cost. The supplied function calculates that shipping cost.

quiz.prompt: Must a Strategy be a subclass?
options: No, a callable can be sufficient
quiz.explanation: A function or callable object can supply the strategy operation.

quiz.prompt: Where should strategy selection usually live?
options: In repeated type checks in each consumer
At a clear composition or call boundary
quiz.explanation: Explicit selection keeps the consumer separate from concrete alternatives.

quiz.prompt: Which issue breaks interchangeability?
options: Unexpected mutation of caller input by one strategy
quiz.explanation: Unexpected changes to caller data can violate the common behavior.

chapters.title: Dependency injection
chapters.subtitle: Dependency injection supplies a component with the objects or functions that it uses.
chapters.body:
## Explicit dependencies
A service that makes its own sender chooses the sender configuration and lifetime. A test must then replace that hidden construction or contact the provider.

Dependency injection supplies the sender from outside, as in WelcomeService(sender). The design can work without a framework. Application setup chooses the concrete sender.

## A small interface
The send operation can be sufficient for a component. The component does not always use a complete application container. A typing.Protocol declaration describes compatible operations without mandatory inheritance.

Protocols mainly support static type checks. They do not automatically validate runtime arguments or prove delivery behavior. A runtime-checkable protocol mainly examines member presence.

## A test implementation
A test sender can keep messages in a list. A test makes the service with that sender and calls the public operation. The recorded message shows the service result without contact with an external provider.

A fixed clock function can similarly supply repeatable time values.

These tests do not prove real authentication, retries, timeouts, or delivery. Those provider requirements must have separate checks.

## Resource lifetime
The creator of a shared connection usually determines when it closes. A consumer must not unexpectedly close it after one operation.

A global service locator hides dependencies again through arbitrary internal lookups. Explicit arguments identify the sender, repository, or function that the component uses.

examples.title: A Protocol and an in-memory collaborator
examples.explanation: The service uses the send operation. The in-memory sender records the result without contact with a provider.
